questions.title: What exactly is 'hyperspherical energy' and why must it be preserved rather than minimized?
questions.question_body: I am reading the section on 'Orthogonal Finetuning' and I am getting confused about the definition and purpose of 'hyperspherical energy'. The paper defines it as $\text{HE}(\bm{W}) := \sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i-\hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$. Intuitively, this looks like a repulsive force between neurons. Why does the paper argue that *preserving* this value is crucial for maintaining semantic ability, whereas previous work (like Liu et al., 2021) tries to *minimize* it? Doesn't minimizing the energy (spreading neurons evenly) lead to better generalization in classification, so shouldn't we do that here too?

questions.title: How does the Cayley parameterization restrict the search space to Special Orthogonal Group SO(d)?
questions.question_body: In the 'Efficient Orthogonal Parameterization' section, the authors propose using $\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(I-\bm{Q})^{-1}$ where $\bm{Q}$ is skew-symmetric. They mention that this only produces orthogonal matrices with determinant 1 (rotations), excluding reflections (det = -1). I understand mathematically why $(I-Q)^{-1}$ combined with $(I+Q)$ yields det=1, but I am unsure if this restriction hurts performance. Did they explicitly test cases where a reflection might be necessary to align features? Or is the intuition that rotations alone are sufficient for the degrees of freedom needed in finetuning?

questions.title: Can someone clarify the exact forward pass difference between OFT and Re-scaled OFT?
questions.question_body: There seems to be a contradiction or at least confusion in Section 4.3 regarding Re-scaled Orthogonal Finetuning. The text states the forward pass is $\bm{z}=(\bm{R}\bm{W}^0\bm{D})^\top\bm{x}$, but then includes a footnote saying: "In the NeurIPS camera ready version, the forward pass... was mistakenly written as $\bm{z}=(\bm{D}\bm{R}\bm{W}^0)^\top\bm{x}$". Since matrix multiplication is not commutative, applying $\bm{D}$ before vs after $\bm{R}$ changes which dimensions are scaled (input features vs output features). Could you confirm which order is actually implemented in their code and whether scaling happens before or after the orthogonal rotation?

questions.title: Why does OFT claim to avoid inference overhead while requiring matrix multiplication at runtime?
questions.question_body: The paper claims in Section 5 ('Intriguing Insights') that 'Unlike ControlNet, our OFT framework introduces no additional inference overhead.' They justify this by saying one can pre-multiply $\bm{R}$ into $\bm{W}^0$ offline to get an equivalent weight matrix $\bm{W}$. However, isn't multiplying two dense matrices ($d \times d$) computationally expensive if done per-layer? If we merge them into a single weight matrix during training/finetuning setup, doesn't that increase memory usage for storing the merged weights compared to just storing $\bm{W}^0$ plus a small low-rank factor like LoRA? How does this scale compared to keeping separate parameters?

questions.title: Is COFT strictly a subset of OFT or an independent method with different optimization objectives?
questions.question_body: Looking at Equation ~eq:coft_general~, COFT adds a constraint $|| \bm{R}- \bm{I} || \leq \epsilon$ on top of orthogonality. This seems like it restricts OFT further. But then they say COFT allows us to tune flexibility via $\\epsilon$. If I set $\\epsilon$ very large, does COFT become identical to standard OFT? And conversely, if I set $\\epsilon=0$, does it revert to doing nothing (just using pretrained weights)? I want to make sure I understand if COFT is just OFT with a regularization term added to the loss function or if it fundamentally changes how gradients flow through the Cayley parameterization.
